questions.text: Describe the steps of the scientific method, in order, using a real-life example to illustrate each step.
questions.answer: The steps are: (1) Observation — Notice that wet clothes dry faster on a windy day. (2) Question — Does wind speed up the drying of clothes? (3) Hypothesis — More wind makes water evaporate faster from clothes. (4) Experiment — Hang two same-sized wet cloths in two places, one in front of a fan and one in still air; check both at the same intervals. (5) Record results — Note how long each takes to dry. (6) Analyse — Compare the times. (7) Conclusion — If the cloth in the fan dried faster, the hypothesis is supported. (8) Communicate — Share findings with classmates.
questions.explanation: Tests whether the student can map each step to a concrete example.

questions.text: Design a fair experiment to compare which fabric (cotton or polyester) absorbs more water. Mention variables, materials, steps, and what you'd measure.
questions.answer: Independent variable: type of fabric. Dependent variable: amount of water absorbed (or weight gain). Controlled variables: same size of fabric piece, same time submerged, same starting temperature of water. Materials: equal pieces of cotton and polyester, water, beam balance, water container, stopwatch. Steps: weigh each dry piece (W1). Submerge each piece in water for 2 minutes. Lift, gently squeeze the same way, weigh again (W2). Calculate water absorbed = W2 - W1 for each. Repeat 3 times, take the average. The fabric with the larger average gain absorbs more water.
questions.explanation: Tests applying fair-test design to a new question.

questions.text: A school wants to start a 'Young Scientists Club'. Design a one-page plan describing 3 weekly activities, the kind of skills each builds, and how students will share their findings.
questions.answer: Week 1 — Garden Investigation: students choose a plant, take weekly measurements (height, leaf count), and note weather. Builds observation, measurement, and recording skills. Week 2 — Mystery Box: each pair gets a sealed box; without opening it, they hypothesise what's inside from sound and weight, then test their guess by checking. Builds hypothesis-formation and reasoning. Week 3 — Kitchen Science: students design a test for which juice keeps an apple slice from browning. Builds experimental design and fair-test skills. Sharing: end-of-month 'science fair' where each pair presents their question, what they did, what they found, and a short reflection.
questions.explanation: Open-ended; full credit for any creative plan with the listed parts.
